articles.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
articles.summary: What is “the true cost of a token”?
articles.full_text:
Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months.

All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok .

June 26, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna.

Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50 , while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10 .

They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.

June 30, 2026 # Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed.

Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.

July 24, 2026 # Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol).

Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.

July 30, 2026 # OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02 .

August 10, 2026 # Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.

August 21, 2026 # OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ( $4 / $20 / $0.40 ) for the next three months.

September 1, 2026 # Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%.

Cache read costs When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn.

Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider).

Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!

September 3, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost.

Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.

September 22, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol!

They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version.

On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”.

Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).

September 29, 2026 # It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.

Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago.

These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code .

More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts.

From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other.

However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play.

So, what gives?

The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure # If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes.

Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent , or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter , and as a result there is little moat.

Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta —who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure.

For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1 , which also recently released an updated 1017 variant .

The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time.

That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised.

I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models.

Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise ( 45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24 ) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003 .

Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”.

On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request.

Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter.

For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers .

However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise.

OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D.

Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs.

Opus 5.5 at 58 ) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ( $2 / $10 / $0.20 ).

It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price.

Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ( $3 / $15 / $0.30 ).

One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends.

The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s , but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high.

As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more .

It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet .

The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic.

As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too.

The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.

On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts.

IPO Pumping # The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon— OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months .

So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months.

Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around.

So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%?

That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus!

The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats.

How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts?

Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave.

I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets .

Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?

I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice.

In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models.

For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.

I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon.

I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models.

After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.

I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced.

Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it.

One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures.

However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline.

Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining!

Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct.

Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die.

Max Woolf (@minimaxir) is formerly a Senior Data Scientist at BuzzFeed in San Francisco who works with AI/ML tools and open source projects.

Max’s projects are funded by his Patreon .

articles.summary: The NIST elliptic curves have been in the news twice lately. A few days ago Anthropic posted a paper on the NIST curve seeds that I wrote about here. Now the curves are in the news again, this time over broken certificates. My post a few days ago was about the possibility that the NSA […] The post Backdoors, Incompetence, and Elliptic Curves first appeared on John D. Cook .
articles.full_text:
The NIST elliptic curves have been in the news twice lately.

A few days ago Anthropic posted a paper on the NIST curve seeds that I wrote about here .

Now the curves are in the news again, this time over broken certificates.

My post a few days ago was about the possibility that the NSA had added a backdoor to the NIST curves.

Anthropic researchers showed that this wasn’t the case.

The NSA had not been able to defend how the curve seeds were chosen because they forgot, but researchers from Anthropic were able to reverse engineer the source of the seeds.

So apparently the NIST curves do not have a backdoor, but as with all encryption, the Achilles heel is human error. eMudrha was using the NIST curve P-384 with extremely small keys: 4, 56, 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237.

To understand why this is a problem, I’ll briefly describe how elliptic curve cryptography works.

P-384 is an elliptic curve designed by NIST, with input from the NSA, for use in cryptography.

The curve has on the order of 2 384 points because the base field is the integers mod p = 2 384 − 2 128 − 2 96 + 2 32 − 1, a 384-bit prime number.

Given a basepoint b on the curve and an exponent e , it is practically impossible to recover e from b e .

That’s the discrete logarithm problem [1], the basis for the security of elliptic curve cryptography.

If and when cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive, the discrete logarithm problem will be solvable and elliptic curve cryptography will be broken.

Until the advent of quantum computing, elliptic curve cryptography is presumably safe, unless someone does something negligent, such as using a tiny value of e like 4.

If e is chosen at random from a group with on the order of 2 384 elements, you cannot recover e from b e without brute force.

But apparently someone said Let’s see.

Is e = 1?

Is it 2?

Is it 3?

Is it 4?

Why yes: e = 4.

Ordinarily this would be hopeless.

You can’t just try 2 384 exponents.

But someone thought to test whether the keys were horrifically bad, and they were right.   [1] The exponentiation here is not over the integers, or over the integers mod p .

It’s over the group structure of the elliptic curve, and that is what makes it hard to compute the discrete logarithm.

articles.title: Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing
articles.summary: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more about AI's impact on the web, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started The digital publishing industry has relied on […]
articles.full_text:
Column AI The Stepback Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing Publishers spent years figuring out how to get clicks on Google.

But new AI search features have torn that ecosystem apart. by Emma Roth Oct 25, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Column AI The Stepback Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing Publishers spent years figuring out how to get clicks on Google.

But new AI search features have torn that ecosystem apart. by Emma Roth Oct 25, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

This is The Stepback , a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world.

For more about AI’s impact on the web, follow Emma Roth .

The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET.

Opt in for The Stepback here .

How it started The digital publishing industry has relied on Google for a very long time.

Many outlets spent time and money optimizing their webpages to show up at the top of the search engine, with the goal of getting readers to click on their articles or discover their websites for the first time.

For years, the relationship between Google and publishers was largely reciprocal; online publishers filled out Google’s search index with content, while Google supplied publications with exposure and traffic.

But that relationship has changed.

The launch of Google’s AI search features — coupled with changes to the way it ranks search results — has made it harder for publishers to survive on traffic from Google alone.

In 2024, Google rolled out AI Overviews, a feature that slots an AI-generated search result summarizing pages from across the web at the very top of Google Search, with links to sources its AI system determines to be the most useful placed below the summary.

Instead of vying for clicks on the first page of Search, publishers became beholden to an AI system that regurgitates results, with no guarantee that users will actually click on the source of that information.

Though Google’s AI Overviews got off to a shaky start , the feature immediately raised concerns among publishers, with the News/Media Alliance saying it will be “catastrophic” to web traffic.

A 2024 investigation from the Press Gazette found that Google’s AI Overviews appeared for almost a quarter of news-related searches in May 2024.

By August, the outlet found that AI Overviews had begun impacting the visibility of publishers by replacing media sites that previously held the top spots on Google’s search engine for certain queries.

A future where Google could eventually stop sending traffic to outside sites on the web has only gotten closer as the company builds out its vision for an AI-powered search.

In May 2025, it launched AI Mode , a feature that replaces Google’s standard search engine with a chatbot-like interface that provides detailed summaries from results on the web.

How it’s going The concerns raised by the News/Media Alliance were real: Traffic to online publishers tanked following the launch of Google’s AI search features.

A June 2025 report from The Wall Street Journal revealed how traffic to Business Insider , The Washington Post , HuffPost , and the WSJ itself has declined since 2022.

Data from analytics company Similarweb suggested that search traffic to The New York Times sank from 44 percent to 35.5 percent in three years, the WSJ reported.

A report from Digiday pointed to similar dips at Digital Content Next (DCN), a trade association that represents outlets and media companies like Bloomberg , The Associated Press , The New York Times , Condé Nast, and Vox Media.

Between May and June 2025, DCN says 19 of its members experienced a traffic loss on Google, ranging from 1 to 25 percent, Digiday reported.

DMG Media, which owns Daily Mail and Metro , told the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority that click-through rates dropped by up to 89 percent between June and July 2025, citing impacts from AI Overviews.

On top of all of this, Pew Research found that people are “less likely” to click on links to other websites when they see an AI Overview.

These numbers starkly contrast with Google’s claims that its AI search features are helping the web.

Last year, Google Search head Liz Reid said click volume from the search engine remained “relatively stable,” adding that AI search is sending more clicks to different types of websites — especially those “with forums, videos, podcasts, and posts” from other users.

Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice president of knowledge and information, told the BBC , “From our point of view, the web is thriving.” In addition to scrutiny from regulators , publishers from around the globe have filed lawsuits against Google, claiming the company’s AI search features have negatively impacted traffic.

Many lawsuits haven’t been successful.

US District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed an antitrust case from Chegg and Penske Media , which owns The Rolling Stone , Billboard , The Hollywood Reporter , and The Verge .

The same judge also rejected a proposed class action lawsuit surrounding AI Overviews filed by Arkansas newspapers.

What happens next Online publishers have had to adjust their strategies in the wake of falling search traffic, with many leaning on social media, newsletters, and subscriptions to promote and make money from their work.

Others are using a toggle that allows them to opt out of appearing in AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting their visibility in search — an option Google broadly rolled out following an order from the UK .

But this still doesn’t fix sinking traffic.

Pushback from online publishers appears to have resulted in some changes to Google’s AI search features.

The company has begun to make sources more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews , as hovering over a link in either feature will show a pop-up with a list of articles and accompanying images.

Another AI search change puts in-line links “higher up in responses more frequently.” Google will likely continue making changes to how it presents sources in AI search, while coming up with ways to compensate publishers that inform its results.

The company says 400 publishers , including The Washington Post , CNN, Axios , and the Financial Times, are now part of its News AI pilot program, which licenses content to develop new AI features.

It’s also testing a program that pays publishers for the use of their content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, according to reports from The Information and Digiday .

Whether this program is enough to repair Google’s relationship with publishers remains to be seen.

By the way Google is burying blue links even further beneath AI Overviews.

The search summaries have started to automatically expand for some queries, instead of requiring users to manually click a “Show more” button.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Reddit is also considering cutting off Google due to dropping traffic.

It’s not just publishers and online forums that are concerned about AI Overviews — the nonprofit Common Sense Media claims the search summaries pose an “unacceptable” risk to kids by failing to respond appropriately to children in crisis.
